en: Praise of the Peerless One: O Peerless One, homage to you who teach the meaning of the absence of intrinsic nature;
you who are intent upon the welfare of this world that is ruined by false views. (1)
Indeed, nothing at all has been seen by you with the Buddha-eye;
yet, O Protector, your vision is unsurpassed, seeing the reality of the ultimate truth.
In the ultimate sense, there is neither an awakener nor that which is to be awakened here;
oh, you have realized the nature of phenomena, which is so exceedingly difficult to understand! (3)
Not a single dharma has been produced by you, nor has any been ceased;
by the very vision of equality, the unsurpassed state has been attained.
Noble Lord, you did not seek nirvāṇa as something superior to saṃsāra;
you attained peace because you found no fault in saṃsāra.
You have realized the single flavor of both affliction and purification;
because of the indivisibility of the realm of phenomena (dharmadhātu), you are pure in every respect.
Not even a single syllable was uttered by you, O Lord;
yet the entire assembly of those to be trained has been satisfied by the rain of Dharma.
You have no attachment to the aggregates, nor to the elements or sense-bases;
with a mind equal to space, you are independent of all phenomena.
O Protector, the notion of a "sentient being" does not arise for you in any way whatsoever;
yet, toward sentient beings afflicted by suffering, you are exceedingly compassionate in nature.
O Lord, your intellect does not become attached to various conceptual constructions such as pleasure and pain, self and non-self, permanence and impermanence, and so forth. (10)
"It is your conviction that there is no going and no coming of phenomena whatsoever;
you who know the ultimate meaning of the Dharma have declared that they are not found gathered anywhere. (11)
You are omnipresent, yet you have not gone anywhere;
O great sage, you are inconceivable in terms of birth, nature, and body.
O blameless one, you have realized that the world is devoid of unity and difference, comparable to an echo, and subject to transition and destruction. 13.
O Lord, you have realized that cyclic existence is devoid of permanence and annihilation, and is free from both the characterized and the characteristics, like a dream or an illusion. (14)
The rivers of afflictions, extending as far as their very root in latent impressions, have been conquered by you;
and from the very nature of those afflictions, the nectar of immortality has been attained. (15)
O steadfast one, you have perceived form as being without characteristics, like that which is formless;
yet you appear within the realm of form with a body radiant with the primary marks.
You are not said to be "seen" by seeing form;
you are well-seen through the vision of Dharma, yet the nature of phenomena (dharmatā) is not seen.
Your body is not of a hollow nature, nor is it composed of flesh, bone, or blood;
like a rainbow, you have manifested a body that is devoid of [material substance]. (18)
There is no disease nor impurity in your body, nor is there any arising of hunger or thirst;
yet, for the sake of conforming to the world, you have displayed worldly activity.
O sinless one, the fault of karmic obstruction does not exist for you in any way;
out of compassion for the world, you have demonstrated the web of karma.
O Lord, because the realm of phenomena (dharmadhātu) is undifferentiated, there is no distinction between vehicles;
yet you have taught the three vehicles for the sake of introducing sentient beings [to the path]. (21)
O Jina, your body is eternal, stable, auspicious, and composed of the Dharma;
yet, for the sake of those to be trained, you have demonstrated your passing into nirvana.
Furthermore, in incalculable world-systems, you are beheld by your devotees who long for your passing away, birth, perfect enlightenment, turning of the wheel [of Dharma], and final nirvāṇa.
O Protector, you have no conceit, no conceptual construction, and no movement;
your buddha-activity proceeds in the world effortlessly.
Thus, having scattered flowers of virtue over the Sugata, who is inconceivable and immeasurable, I have attained [this merit].
By this, may all sentient beings here become virtuous.
They are vessels for the most profound Dharma of the Lord of Munis. || 25 ||
The Praise of the Peerless One is completed.
